item.title: Consistency Models, CAP, PACELC and Consensus
item.description:
Simple definition#

A consistency model is a promise about what a read can return after writes, when data is copied across machines. Strong models behave like a single copy. Weaker models allow stale or reordered reads in exchange for latency and availability.

item.title: Data & Security Architect Learning Path
item.description: This path takes you from the event log to a secure, regulated, end-to-end platform design. Each step builds on the previous one. The case studies at the end of each module combine what you have learned into a complete design.

item.title: Modern Data Platform Architecture
item.description:
Simple definition#

A data platform collects data from operational systems, stores it reliably and cheaply, and turns it into trusted data products for reporting, analytics, machine learning and AI. The modern default is a lakehouse: open table formats on object storage, queried by many engines under one governance catalog.

item.title: Apache Kafka Architecture
item.description:
Simple definition#

Apache Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform. At its core it is a replicated, partitioned, append-only log: producers append records, the cluster stores them durably for a configured time, and any number of consumers read them independently. Each consumer can re-read old records whenever it needs to.

item.title: Threat Modelling
item.description:
Simple definition#

Threat modelling is a structured way to answer: what are we building, what can go wrong, what are we going to do about it, and did we do a good job? It finds design-level security and privacy problems early, when fixing them is cheap.

item.title: Data Governance: Catalog, Lineage, Quality and Contracts
item.description:
Simple definition#

Data governance is the set of roles, policies, standards and tools that make sure data is known (catalogued and defined), trusted (good quality with traceable lineage), protected (secure and private) and used properly (meeting regulation and ethics) across its lifecycle.

item.title: Design Review Checklist
item.description:
How to use it#

Use this checklist to review your own design before building, or a team’s design at an architecture board. Score each area 0–3 and record the evidence.

1. Goals and non-functional requirements#

  • Throughput (average and peak), latency budgets, availability, RPO and RTO stated per flow?
  • Which flows are synchronous (the user waits) and which are asynchronous?
  • Red flags: “real-time” undefined; no peak numbers; one SLO for everything.

2. Boundaries and data ownership#

  • Each piece of data has one owning service? No shared databases between services?
  • Do data that must change together live together?
  • Red flags: services reading each other’s tables; every change spans services.

3. Events and contracts#

  • Events named as past-tense facts; integration events separated from internal ones?
  • Keys chosen for ordering; partition count sized for growth?
  • Schemas registered, compatibility mode chosen (transitive if replayed), CI checks in place?
  • No secrets or unnecessary PII in events; trace context propagated?
  • Red flags: schemaless JSON; compatibility NONE; low-cardinality keys; PAN in events.

4. Consistency#

  • Consistency model stated per operation (strong where invariants live, eventual elsewhere)?
  • Invariants protected inside one ACID or consensus boundary?
  • Read-your-writes handled where users need it?
  • Red flags: decisions made on async replicas or read models; “eventually consistent” used as an excuse.

5. Failure handling#

  • Outbox (or equivalent) for state plus event; idempotent consumers; idempotency keys on APIs?
  • Sagas with explicit compensations, timeouts and manual-review paths?
  • Retries with backoff, DLTs, poison-message handling; the timeout (unknown) outcome designed?
  • Reconciliation jobs for money and critical data?
  • Red flags: @Transactional around remote calls; infinite retries; no compensation design.

6. Data platform and governance#

  • Open table formats and one catalog; medallion or product layers defined?
  • Owners, contracts and quality gates per data product; lineage captured automatically?
  • Regulatory reports traceable to source (BCBS 239)?
  • Red flags: copies per tool; no owners; quality checks only on final reports.

7. Data security and privacy#

  • Data classified; sensitive identifiers tokenised early; masking by default?
  • Encryption in transit and at rest with managed keys (HSM/KMS); key separation of duties?
  • ABAC or row and column security; JIT access to restricted data; access recertification?
  • Residency, retention and erasure (including immutable stores) designed?
  • Red flags: production data in test; PII in logs and prompts; “we encrypt the disk” as the only control.

8. Threats and security architecture#

  • Current threat model (DFD, trust boundaries, STRIDE, LINDDUN for personal data)?
  • Zero trust: strong user and workload identity, mTLS, per-object authorisation?
  • Supply chain: SBOM, signing, provenance, admission policy; secrets dynamic and short-lived?
  • Crypto inventory and crypto-agility for PQC?
  • Red flags: trusted internal network; authorisation only at the gateway; long-lived static credentials.

9. AI risk#

  • AI use cases inventoried and classified (EU AI Act tier)?
  • Least agency, user-scoped tools, human approval for consequential actions?
  • Permission-aware RAG; output validation; token and cost limits?
  • Red-teamed and continuously evaluated; traces kept?
  • Red flags: agents with service-account superpowers; security rules only in the system prompt.

10. Compliance and operations#

  • Applicable regulations listed (PCI DSS, DORA, PSD2/3, GDPR/DPDP, RBI, CERT-In, SEBI, AI Act); controls mapped once to many?
  • Incident detection, classification and reporting clocks (4/6/24/72 h) automated and rehearsed?
  • Resilience testing, restore tests, third-party register and exit plans?
  • Monitoring: lag, DLTs, saga states, quality, access anomalies, cost?
  • Red flags: compliance as an annual project; paper-only incident plans; unknown ICT dependencies.

Scoring rubric#

Score Meaning
0 Not considered
1 Considered, but not designed
2 Designed, but not yet verified
3 Designed and verified (tests, evidence, drills)

A design is ready to build at an average of at least 2 with no zeros in areas 4, 5, 7 or 8. It is ready for production at 3 in all applicable areas.

item.title: Kafka Producers, Consumers and Delivery Guarantees
item.description:
Simple definition#

A producer writes records to topic partitions. A consumer reads them and records its progress as offsets. Delivery guarantees describe what happens to a record when something fails in between: it can be lost, duplicated or processed exactly once.

item.title: Security Architecture: Zero Trust, AppSec, Supply Chain and Cryptography
item.description:
Simple definition#

Security architecture is the set of principles, patterns and controls that make a system resist, detect and recover from attacks by design. It covers identity, network, application, data, supply chain, cryptography and operations.

Core principles#

Principle Meaning
Defence in depth Multiple independent layers, so one failure is not a breach
Least privilege Minimum access, for minimum time
Zero trust Never trust by network location; verify explicitly every time
Secure by default Safe settings out of the box; insecure options require effort
Fail securely Errors deny access. This is OWASP A10:2025, “Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions”.
Assume breach Limit blast radius; detect and respond fast
Separation of duties No single person or service can complete a critical action alone
Economy of mechanism Simple designs are easier to verify

Zero trust architecture#

NIST SP 800-207 defines zero trust as moving defences from static network perimeters to users, assets and resources. Every request is authenticated, authorised and encrypted, based on identity and context.

item.title: AI Security: Securing LLM Applications and Agents
item.description:
Simple definition#

AI security protects systems built on machine learning, especially large language models (LLMs) and AI agents, from manipulation, data leakage, misuse and failure. It also protects people and organisations from harm caused by those systems.

item.title: Data Security and Privacy Engineering
item.description:
Simple definition#

Data security protects the confidentiality, integrity and availability of data against unauthorised access, change or loss. Privacy engineering makes sure personal data is collected and used only for legitimate, stated purposes, minimised, and handled according to people’s rights.

item.title: Event-Driven Architecture
item.description:
Simple definition#

In an event-driven architecture (EDA), services announce facts that happened (“PaymentAuthorised”) instead of telling other services what to do. Interested services react to those events in their own time. The producer does not know, or need to know, who is listening.

item.title: Transactional Outbox, CDC and Idempotent Consumers
item.description:
Simple definition#

  • Transactional outbox: write the business change and the event to the same database in one transaction, then publish the event from the database to the broker.
  • Change data capture (CDC): read a database’s transaction log and stream every change as events.
  • Idempotent consumer: a consumer that gives the same result whether a message arrives once or several times.

Together they give effectively-once processing without distributed transactions.

item.title: Data, Distributed Systems & Security Quick Reference
item.description:
Kafka production defaults#

Setting Value
replication.factor 3 (across 3 AZs, rack-aware)
min.insync.replicas 2
acks all
enable.idempotence true
unclean.leader.election.enable false
compression.type zstd or lz4
linger.ms / batch.size 5–20 ms / 64–256 KB
enable.auto.commit (business consumers) false; commit after processing
group.protocol consumer (KIP-848)
isolation.level (downstream of transactions) read_committed
Controllers 3 dedicated KRaft controllers

Delivery semantics#

Need Use
Loss acceptable At-most-once
Business events At-least-once + idempotent consumer
Kafka → process → Kafka Exactly-once (transactions / exactly_once_v2)
DB state + event Transactional outbox + CDC
API retries Idempotency-Key

Which pattern?#

Problem Pattern
State change must emit an event reliably Outbox + CDC
Duplicates Idempotent consumer / inbox
Multi-service business transaction Saga (orchestrated for long flows)
Reserve then commit TCC / authorise–capture
Different read and write shapes CQRS
Full history and audit Event sourcing
Queue of independent jobs Kafka share group
Ordered stream per entity Consumer group, keyed by entity
Real-time aggregates and alerts Flink / Kafka Streams with event time

Consistency cheat sheet#

Term One-liner
Linearizable Behaves like one copy, in real-time order
Causal Causes are seen before effects
Read-your-writes You see your own updates
Eventual Replicas converge when writes stop
CAP Under a partition: C or A
PACELC Else: latency or consistency
Quorum R + W > N
Raft Majority commit; 3 or 5 nodes

Table formats and catalogs#

Iceberg Delta Hudi
Strength Engine-neutral, REST catalog Spark/Databricks Upserts, incremental
Catalogs Polaris, Unity, Glue/S3 Tables, Nessie Unity Hive/Glue

Iceberg v3: deletion vectors · row lineage · VARIANT · geo types · ns timestamps · defaults.

item.title: System Design: A Governed Data Platform for a Bank
item.description:
The design brief#

“A bank operating in the EU and India wants one data platform for regulatory reporting, risk, fraud analytics, customer insights and GenAI. Today it has three warehouses, a Hadoop lake and hundreds of spreadsheet reports with conflicting numbers. Regulators have criticised its risk data aggregation.”

item.title: FinTech Regulations for Architects
item.description:
Simple definition#

FinTech regulations set legally binding requirements for how financial services protect money, data and customers, and how they stay operational. For architects, every regulation turns into non-functional requirements: security controls, data handling, resilience, auditability and reporting timelines.

item.title: The Saga Pattern
item.description:
Simple definition#

A saga is a sequence of local transactions, one per service. If a step fails, the saga runs compensating transactions to semantically undo the steps that already succeeded. It replaces one big distributed transaction with steps that are each atomic, plus an explicit undo plan.

item.title: Schemas, Event Contracts and Evolution
item.description:
Simple definition#

An event contract is the agreed shape and meaning of an event: field names, types, required fields, semantics and service levels. A schema registry stores every version of that shape and checks that new versions do not break existing producers or consumers.

item.title: System Design: A Secure, Compliant Payments Platform
item.description:
The design brief#

“A digital bank operating in the EU and India is launching card and account-to-account payments, an open-banking API for partners, and a GenAI assistant that answers customer questions and can initiate small transfers. Design the security architecture so that it is PCI DSS, DORA, PSD2/PSD3, GDPR/DPDP and RBI compliant, and can withstand a determined attacker.”

item.title: CQRS and Event Sourcing
item.description:
Simple definition#

  • CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation): use one model to change data (commands) and one or more different models to read it (queries).
  • Event sourcing: store every change as an immutable event, and derive current state by replaying them, instead of storing only the latest state.

They are often used together, but each works without the other.

item.title: Stream Processing with Flink and Kafka Streams
item.description:
Simple definition#

Stream processing computes results continuously as events arrive: filtering, enriching, aggregating, joining and detecting patterns. Batch processing instead waits for a complete dataset. The result is another stream, a table or an action, available in milliseconds to seconds.

item.title: System Design: Order Processing Across Microservices
item.description:
The design brief#

“Customers buy products online. An order must reserve stock, take payment and book delivery. Customers track their order in real time. Peak is 2,000 orders per second during sales. We must never charge for an order we cannot fulfil, and never ship an unpaid order.”

item.title: System Design: Event-Driven Real-Time Payments
item.description:
The design brief#

“Design the core of a bank’s instant payments service. Customers send money from mobile and web; payments must settle in under 10 seconds, end to end, 24×7. Each payment must be fraud-checked, posted to the ledger exactly once, notified to both parties and reconciled with the scheme daily.”

item.title: About this handbook
item.description:
Purpose#

The Data, Distributed Systems & Cybersecurity Knowledge Hub explains event streaming, distributed data consistency, data platforms and security architecture simply, with diagrams and flows. It is written for architects, senior engineers, data engineers and security engineers, especially those working in financial services. It is a companion to the Java & Software Architecture Knowledge Hub, the Enterprise AI & Agentic AI Knowledge Hub and the Cloud Native & Platform Engineering Knowledge Hub.

item.title: Glossary
item.description:
Definitions are deliberately short. Follow the links for the full explanations.

A–C#

ABAC (attribute-based access control)
Access decisions from attributes of the user, the data and the context. See Data security.
At-least-once delivery
Messages are never lost but may be duplicated. See Producers and consumers.
BCBS 239
Basel principles for risk data aggregation and reporting. See Data governance.
BOLA
Broken object-level authorisation, the top API security risk. See Security architecture.
CAP theorem
Under a network partition, choose consistency or availability. See Consistency.
CDC (change data capture)
Streaming database changes from the transaction log. See Outbox and CDC.
CDE (cardholder data environment)
Systems that store, process or transmit card data, and so fall in PCI DSS scope. See FinTech regulations.
Compensating transaction
A business action that semantically undoes an earlier saga step. See Saga.
Consumer group
Kafka consumers sharing partitions, one owner per partition. See Kafka architecture.
CQRS
Separate models for commands (writes) and queries (reads). See CQRS and event sourcing.
Crypto-shredding
Making data unreadable by deleting its encryption key. See Data security.

D–I#

Data contract
A producer–consumer agreement covering schema, semantics, quality, SLOs and ownership. See Schemas and contracts.
Data mesh
Domain-owned data products on a self-serve platform with federated governance. See Data platforms.
DORA
The EU Digital Operational Resilience Act for financial entities, applicable since January 2025. See FinTech regulations.
DPDP Act
India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, with Rules notified in 2025. See FinTech regulations.
Envelope encryption
Data encrypted with a data key, and the data key encrypted with a master key in a KMS or HSM. See Data security.
Event sourcing
Storing state as an append-only sequence of events. See CQRS and event sourcing.
Excessive agency
An AI system with more tools, permissions or autonomy than it needs. See AI security.
FAPI 2.0
OpenID Foundation security profile for financial-grade APIs. See Security architecture.
Iceberg
An open table format adding ACID, schema evolution and time travel to files. See Data platforms.
Idempotency
An operation that has the same effect whether applied once or many times. See Outbox and idempotency.
ISR (in-sync replicas)
Kafka replicas caught up with the partition leader. See Kafka architecture.

K–P#

KRaft
Kafka’s built-in Raft metadata quorum, replacing ZooKeeper since 4.0. See Kafka architecture.
Lakehouse
Open table formats on object storage, queried by many engines under one catalog. See Data platforms.
Lineage
The record of where data came from and how it was transformed. See Data governance.
LINDDUN
A privacy threat-modelling method. See Threat modelling.
Linearizability
The strongest single-object consistency: behaves like one copy in real-time order. See Consistency.
Medallion architecture
Bronze (raw), silver (conformed) and gold (product) data layers. See Data platforms.
MITRE ATLAS
A knowledge base of adversarial techniques against AI systems. See AI security.
Outbox pattern
Writing state and event in one local transaction, and relaying the event later. See Outbox.
PACELC
Partition: availability or consistency; else: latency or consistency. See Consistency.
PCI DSS
The security standard for cardholder data; v4.0.1 is current. See FinTech regulations.
Post-quantum cryptography (PQC)
Algorithms resistant to quantum attacks (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA). See Security architecture.
Prompt injection
Instructions in input or content that manipulate an LLM. See AI security.

R–Z#

Raft
A consensus protocol using leader election and majority log replication. See Consistency.
Saga
A sequence of local transactions with compensations. See Saga.
SBOM
A software bill of materials: an inventory of components. See Security architecture.
SCA (strong customer authentication)
Two of knowledge, possession and inherence, required by PSD2. See FinTech regulations.
Schema registry
A service that stores schema versions and enforces compatibility. See Schemas and contracts.
Share group
Queue-style Kafka consumption with per-record acknowledgement (KIP-932). See Kafka architecture.
SLSA
Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts: build integrity and provenance. See Security architecture.
STRIDE
Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege. See Threat modelling.
TCC (Try–Confirm–Cancel)
Reserve resources, then confirm or cancel them. See Distributed transactions.
Tokenisation
Replacing sensitive values with random tokens mapped in a secure vault. See Data security.
Watermark
A stream processor’s estimate of event-time progress, used to close windows. See Stream processing.
Zero trust
No implicit trust from network location; verify every request. See Security architecture.
